### Problem 1

##OH questions: 1. Do we get rid of NA's? 2. guidance on indicating the extent to which missing data is issue - key points to look at/mention? 3. what does 'reasonable units' mean, do the 3 variables have to be converted to imperial? 4. what is 'structure' asking for 5. why is scatterplot not the best option?6. When we look at 0-100 for snowfall, is it by the original or is it by new variables we created

**Step 1: import and clean data**
```{r import}
data("ny_noaa") #load dataset into environment

noaa_df <- ny_noaa #assign into df, no need to convert missing values to NA since it's 'pre-built' into file

noaa_df = janitor::clean_names(noaa_df)

print(noaa_df, n = 20) #shows that column names converted correctly and that first 16 rows contains no data

```
**Preliminary Data description:**
This dataset contains `r ncol(noaa_df)` variables named: "id", "date", "prcp", "snow", "snwd", "tmax" and "tmin". In these 7 columns, it contains `r nrow(noaa_df)` observations with its weather station ID ("id"), date of observation ("date"), precipitation to tenths of mm ("prcp"), snowfall to mm ("snow"), snow depth to mm ("snwd"), and min max temperature to tenths of Celsius ("tmin", "tmax"). The extent to which missing data is an issue depends on what questions you want to answer as well as if the data missing can be inferred from other data in the same row. For example if you want to ask about precipitation levels for a certain time period in which the column 'prcp' is empty, then that would be a major issue. However, variables like 'snwd' could probably be inferred from 'snow'. Especially with `r nrow(noaa_df)` amount of entries even if you can't directly calculate 'snwd' given 'snow', you can just look at other entries with the same 'snow' value and copy it in. These are just two examples to show that missing data can be a very big issue or a relatively smaller one depending on your question and specific circumstances. 

**Step 2: Data Manipulation**
```{r noaa_manipulation}
noaa_df <- ny_noaa %>% #This creates separate variables for year, month and day and converts observations of temperature, precipitation and snowfall into more convenient scales (from mm or tenths of mm to cm and from tenths of degrees celsius to degrees celsius) 
  mutate(year = year(date),
         month = month(date),
         day = day(date),
         tmax_1deg = as.numeric(tmax)/10, #1C = 10 tengths of degrees celsius
         tmin_1deg = as.numeric(tmin)/10, #1C = 10 tengths of degrees celsius
         prcp_cm = prcp/100, #1 cm = 100 tenths of mm
         snow_cm = snow/10, #1 cm = 10 mm
         snwd_cm = snwd/10) #1 cm = 10 mm

print(n = 20, noaa_df, width = Inf)#Checked to see that new columns (variables) made correctly. 

mc_snow <- noaa_df %>%
  count(snow_cm) %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 1) 

mc_snwd <- noaa_df %>%
  count(snwd_cm) %>%
  slice_max(n, n = 1)# shows results in tibble, most common value for both is '0' and shows up 1597641 times. 

mc_snowil <- mc_snow %>%
  pull(snow_cm)

mc_snwdil <- mc_snwd %>%
  pull(snwd_cm)
```
**Comment:**
For snowfall, the most common values for "snow_cm" and "snwd_cm" are `r mc_snowil` and `r mc_snwdil` respectively. This is because in New York where the weather data is being collected, most days out of the year don't snow. 

**Step 3: Data Visualization**
```{r noaa_visualization}
#January plot: 
jan_noaa <- noaa_df %>%
  filter(month == 1) %>%
  group_by(id, year) %>%
  summarize(mean_tmax = mean(tmax_1deg, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.2, colour = "steelblue") +
  labs(
    title = "Average Maximum Temperature in Janurary 1981-2010",
    x ="", 
    y = "Avg max Temp (°C)"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
#July plot: 
july_noaa <- noaa_df %>%
filter(month == 7) %>%
  group_by(id, year) %>%
  summarize(mean_tmax = mean(tmax_1deg, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.2, color = "tomato") +
  labs(
    title = "Average Maximum Temperature in July 1981-2010",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Avg max Temp (°C)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# 3. Combine using patchwork operators
jan_noaa / july_noaa
```
There doesn't seem to be any trend with temperatures within the same ranges (about -5 to 10C for Jan and 20-30C for July) across the period observed (1981-2010). However, the stations generally trend up and down 'together' and so we see bold thick lines going up and down together. However, outliers do exist trending at times opposite to the majority instead of just trending 'too much' in the direction of the majority. Examples include the two large downward spikes between 1980-1990 in the "July" plot and a few peaks upwards between 2000-2005 in the "January" plot. 

**Step 3 cont: Data Visualization**
```{r p2}
p1 <- noaa_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin_1deg, y = tmax_1deg)) +
  geom_bin2d(bins = 60) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(option = "viridis")
  labs(
    title = "Panel (i): Maximum vs. Minimum Temperature",
    x = "Min Temperature (°C)",
    y = "Max Temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Count"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

p2 <- noaa_df %>%
  filter(snow > 0 & snow < 100) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = snow)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "skyblue", color = "darkblue", alpha = 0.6, outlier.alpha = 0.1) +
  labs(
    title = "Panel (ii): Snowfall Distribution by Year (0 < Snowfall < 100)",
    x = "Year",
    y = "Snowfall (mm)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1) # Tilt year labels for readability
  )

# Combine them vertically using patchwork
p1 / p2
```
### Problem 2
**Step 1: Load, tidy and merge**
```{r import2}
acc_df <- read_csv(file = "./data/nhanes_accel.csv",
                   na = c("", "NA", "."))|>
          janitor::clean_names()

demo_df <- read_csv(file = "./data/nhanes_covar.csv",
                    skip = 4,
                    na = c("", "NA", "."))|>
          janitor::clean_names() |>
          drop_na() |>
          filter(age >= 21)
          
print(acc_df)
print(demo_df) #this is to check that the skip = 4, na conversions, drop_na, age < 21 dropped, clean_names all worked

demo_df <- demo_df %>%
  mutate(
    # Convert sex: 1 = male, 2 = female
    sex = factor(sex, 
                 levels = c(1, 2), 
                 labels = c("Male", "Female")),
    
    # Convert education: 1 = less than highschool, 2 = highschool equivalent, 3 = more than highschool
    education = factor(education, 
                       levels = c(1, 2, 3), 
                       labels = c("Less than high school", 
                                  "High school equivalent", 
                                  "More than high school"))
  )

merged_df <- demo_df %>%
  full_join(acc_df, by = "seqn")

print(n = 25, merged_df) #shows properly merged, clean and tidy df ready for manipulation
```
**Step 2: Table Creation**
```{r table}
edu_by_sex <- merged_df %>%
  drop_na(sex, education) %>%
  count(education, sex) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = n, values_fill = 0)

print(edu_by_sex) #Checks that table works

knitr::kable(
  edu_by_sex,
  col.names = c("Education Category", "Male", "Female"),
  caption = "Table 1. Number of Men and Women Across Education Categories"
)

male1 <- edu_by_sex %>%
  filter(education == 'Less than high school') %>%
  pull(Male)

male2 <- edu_by_sex %>%
  filter(education == 'High school equivalent') %>%
  pull(Male)

male3 <- edu_by_sex %>%
  filter(education == 'More than high school') %>%
  pull(Male)

female1 <- edu_by_sex %>%
  filter(education == 'Less than high school') %>%
  pull(Female)

female2 <- edu_by_sex %>%
  filter(education == 'High school equivalent') %>%
  pull(Female)

female3  <- edu_by_sex %>%
  filter(education == 'More than high school') %>%
  pull(Female)

```
**Comment on Male and Female by Education Cat Table:**
From the table, we see that males and females with less than high school education are `r male1` and `r female1` respectively. males and females with high school equivalent education are `r male2` and `r female2` respectively and finally, males and females with higher than highs school education are `r male3` and `r female3` respectively. The dataset is mostly balanced between Male and Female with the greatest difference being `r male2-female2` between Male and Female who received high school equivalent education. 
**Step 3: Visualization**
```{r agedist_visualization}
#Create the visualization for age distributions
age_dist_plot <- merged_df %>%
  drop_na(age, sex, education) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = education, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.7, outlier.alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution by Education Category and Sex",
    x = "Education Category",
    y = "Age (Years)",
    fill = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 20, hjust = 1), # Tilt text slightly if labels are long
    legend.position = "bottom"
  ) +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2")

# Print the plot
print(age_dist_plot)
```
**Comment on age distribution by education cat and sex plot:**
The mean ages for each education category between the 2 sexes are quite similar. With the 'Less than high school' category having a mean female age of `r merged_df %>% filter(education == "Less than high school", sex == "Female") %>% summarize(mean_age = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull(mean_age) %>% round(1)` and a mean male age of `r merged_df %>% filter(education == "Less than high school", sex == "Male") %>% summarize(mean_age = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull(mean_age) %>% round(1)`. Then in the 'High school equivalent' category, the mean female age is `r merged_df %>% filter(education == "High school equivalent", sex == "Female") %>% summarize(mean_age = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull(mean_age) %>% round(1)` while the mean male age is `r merged_df %>% filter(education == "High school equivalent", sex == "Male") %>% summarize(mean_age = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull(mean_age) %>% round(1)`. Finally in the 'More than Highschool' category, the mean female age is `r merged_df %>% filter(education == "More than high school", sex == "Female") %>% summarize(mean_age = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull(mean_age) %>% round(1)` while the mean male age is `r merged_df %>% filter(education == "More than high school", sex == "Male") %>% summarize(mean_age = mean(age, na.rm = TRUE)) %>% pull(mean_age) %>% round(1)`. The range of ages goes from about 30 upwards to about 75 across education categories and sex. There is also a downwards trend in mean age observable in both sexes from the 'less than highschool' category until the youngest category of 'more than highschool'.
